title: Headworks of storage plants
summary: Gravity dam stability rests on three checks — no tension (e less than or equal to B/6), sliding, and overturning — and the elementary profile follows directly from the no-tension condition. For the spillway, the reason the ogee profile is shaped as it is deserves understanding: it follows the lower nappe of a freely falling jet, so the pressure on the crest stays atmospheric and cavitation cannot occur. Earth dam questions turn on the phreatic line and on the fact that overtopping, not seepage, is the leading cause of failure.

sections.heading: Types of dam and their selection
sections.body:
| Type | Resists water load by | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **Gravity dam** | Its **own weight** | A sound **rock** foundation; any height; a narrow or wide valley |
| **Earth fill (embankment) dam** | Weight; a **flexible** structure | **Any foundation**, including soft; where earth is abundant and rock scarce |
| **Rockfill dam** | Weight, with an impervious membrane or core | Where rock is abundant; steep valleys |
| **Arch dam** | **Transmitting thrust to the abutments** | A **narrow gorge with very strong rock abutments** |
| **Buttress / hollow gravity** | Weight plus the buttresses' stiffness | Saves concrete; needs good foundation |
| Barrage / weir | — | **Diversion only**, no storage |

**Selecting the type** — the decisive factors:

| Factor | Influence |
|---|---|
| **Foundation** | **Sound rock → gravity or arch. Soft or variable → EARTH FILL** |
| **Valley shape** | **Narrow gorge with strong abutments → ARCH** (most economical in material). Wide valley → earth fill |
| **Materials available** | Earth or rock nearby → embankment; aggregate and cement available → concrete |
| **Spillway** | An earth dam **cannot be overtopped**, so it needs a **separate spillway**, often on an abutment; a concrete dam can carry the spillway over itself |
| **Seismicity** | A well-built **earth fill dam performs well** in earthquakes (it deforms); a rigid dam must be designed for the dynamic load |
| Height, cost, time | — |

**The foundation is the governing factor**, and the reason is direct: a gravity or arch dam concentrates its load on a small footprint and cannot tolerate differential settlement, so it needs rock. An **earth fill dam spreads its load over a wide base** and, being flexible, tolerates settlement — so it can be built where a concrete dam cannot. That is why the great majority of the world's dams are embankments.

**Nepal's situation** favours embankment and concrete gravity types in most valleys, with the added constraints that **arch dams need abutment rock of a quality the fractured Himalayan geology rarely offers**, and that **seismic design** is mandatory everywhere. **Kulekhani** is Nepal's principal storage project, and its history illustrates the sedimentation risk discussed below.

**Terminology for a dam:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Heel** | The **upstream** edge of the base |
| **Toe** | The **downstream** edge |
| **Crest** | The top |
| Free board | Crest level above the maximum water level |
| **Full Reservoir Level (FRL)** | The maximum level at which water is stored |
| **Maximum Water Level (MWL)** | FRL plus the surcharge during the design flood |
| **Minimum Drawdown Level (MDDL)** | The lowest operating level; below it is dead storage |
| Galleries | Internal passages for drainage, grouting and inspection |

sections.heading: Gravity dam analysis
sections.body:
**Forces acting on a gravity dam:**

| Force | Direction and note |
|---|---|
| **Self weight W** | Downward through the centroid — **the stabilising force** |
| **Water pressure P** | Horizontal, **½γH²** acting at **H/3** above the base |
| **UPLIFT (pore) pressure U** | **Upward on the base** — reduces the effective weight |
| **Silt pressure** | Horizontal, from deposited sediment; uses the **submerged** unit weight and a coefficient of earth pressure |
| **Earthquake forces** | Horizontal and vertical **inertia** on the dam, plus **hydrodynamic** pressure from the reservoir |
| Wave pressure | On the upper part of the face |
| Ice pressure | Not usually relevant in Nepal at dam elevations |
| Wind | Negligible |

**Uplift is the force that most reduces stability**, and it is worth understanding as such: water seeping into the foundation and the dam–rock contact acts **upward on the base**, effectively **reducing the dam's weight** — which is the only thing holding it in place. Halving the effective weight halves the resistance to both sliding and overturning.

**Uplift is reduced by:**

| Measure | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Grout curtain** near the heel | **Lengthens the seepage path**, reducing the pressure that reaches the base |
| **Drainage gallery with drain holes** | **Intercepts the seepage and relieves the pressure** behind the curtain |
| Foundation treatment, consolidation grouting | Reduces the permeability generally |

The **grout curtain and drainage gallery work as a pair** — the curtain resists the flow, the drains relieve whatever gets past it — and together they can reduce the uplift at the drain line to a fraction of the full reservoir head. Their omission or blockage has caused dam failures, which is why the gallery is inspected and the drains cleaned as routine operation.

**The three stability checks:**

**1. No tension (the middle-third rule):**

> **e ≤ B/6**, so the resultant falls within the **middle third** of the base
> **σ = ΣV/B (1 ± 6e/B)**

Because concrete and the dam–rock contact **cannot carry tension**, tension at the heel would open a crack, which would then admit full reservoir pressure into it — increasing the uplift, propagating the crack further, and leading to failure. The no-tension rule prevents that chain from starting.

**2. Sliding:**

> **Factor of safety against sliding = μ ΣV / ΣH ≥ 1.5**
> **Shear friction factor = (μ ΣV + c A)/ΣH ≥ 3 to 5** (including the cohesion of the contact)

**3. Overturning:**

> **Factor of safety = Σ stabilising moments / Σ overturning moments ≥ 1.5** (about the toe)

**4. Crushing:** the maximum compressive stress at the toe must not exceed the permissible stress of the concrete or the rock.

**The elementary profile.** Applying the no-tension condition to a triangular dam of height H gives the minimum base width:

> **B = H / √(S_c − c)**

where **S_c** is the specific gravity of the dam material (about 2.4) and **c** the uplift coefficient. With **no uplift (c = 0)** this reduces to the classic

> **B = H / √S_c**

and with full uplift (c = 1) to **B = H/√(S_c − 1)**, which is markedly wider — a direct quantitative illustration of how much uplift costs.

**Modes of failure** of a gravity dam: **overturning**, **sliding**, **crushing (compression failure)**, **tension cracking**, and **failure of the foundation** — the last being the commonest in practice, since a dam is usually stronger than the rock it stands on.

**Seismic analysis.** The horizontal earthquake force acts as an inertia force **αW** on the dam plus a **hydrodynamic pressure** on the upstream face, given by **Zangar's** or **Westergaard's** method. The critical point is that the earthquake inertia acts **upstream or downstream**, and the **downstream-acting case combines with the water load** to give the worst condition — while the **upstream-acting case with an empty reservoir** can produce tension at the toe. Both must be checked.

**Galleries** in a gravity dam serve several purposes at once: **drainage** (the foundation drainage gallery), **grouting** access, **inspection**, **instrumentation** (piezometers, strain gauges, seismographs), and **access to gates and valves**. They also, incidentally, reduce the concrete volume.

sections.heading: Spillways and energy dissipation
sections.body:
**A spillway passes the flood safely**, and its adequacy is a matter of dam safety rather than economy: a spillway too small means the dam is **overtopped**, which for an earth dam means failure.

**Types:**

| Spillway | Character |
|---|---|
| **Ogee (overflow)** | The **standard for a concrete dam**; the crest is shaped to the lower nappe profile |
| **Chute (trough)** | A steep open channel on an abutment; suits an **earth dam** |
| **Side channel** | A channel parallel to the crest; where the abutment is narrow |
| **Shaft (morning glory)** | A circular crest leading to a vertical shaft and tunnel; where space is very limited |
| **Siphon** | Self-priming; **automatic**, maintains a nearly constant level, but small capacity |
| Emergency / fuse plug | Deliberately erodible section, for a flood beyond the design |

**The ogee profile — why it is shaped as it is**, and this is the most examined conceptual item:

> The ogee crest is shaped to follow the **LOWER NAPPE of a freely falling jet** issuing from a sharp-crested weir at the design head.

**The consequence is that at the design head the water follows the surface exactly, so:**

| Property | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Pressure on the crest stays ATMOSPHERIC** | The water is neither pressed against the surface nor pulled away from it |
| **No NEGATIVE pressure**, hence **no CAVITATION** | Negative pressure would cause vapour bubbles that collapse and pit the concrete |
| **No separation**, so the **full discharge capacity** is realised | A separated jet loses capacity and produces vibration |

**At heads above the design head** the jet tends to pull away from the surface, producing **sub-atmospheric pressure** and cavitation risk; at heads **below** it, the water presses on the crest, reducing efficiency slightly but safely. So the design head is chosen with that asymmetry in mind, and profiles are sometimes designed for a head slightly below the maximum for that reason.

**Discharge over an ogee spillway:**

> **Q = C L H^{3/2}**  with **C ≈ 2.2** (metric) for a free-flowing ogee

Note the **exponent 3/2**, as for every rectangular-type weir. An option offering **√H** for a spillway is offering an impossible exponent.

**Gated or ungated:**

| | **Ungated (free overflow)** | **Gated** |
|---|---|---|
| Operation | **None required** — fail-safe | Needs operation and power |
| Storage | Crest fixes the FRL | Gates allow **storage above the crest**, gaining useful capacity |
| Flood passage | Automatic | Requires correct operation |
| Reliability | **Highest** | Depends on gates and operators |

Gates gain valuable storage but introduce the risk that they are **not opened in time** — a cause of several dam failures worldwide. The design response is redundancy: multiple gates, independent power, manual operation capability, and clear operating rules.

**Energy dissipation** at the spillway toe. Water arrives with enormous energy that will scour the river bed and undermine the dam if not dissipated in a controlled place.

| Method | Suits |
|---|---|
| **Stilling basin (hydraulic jump)** | Adequate tailwater available |
| **Ski-jump / flip bucket** | **High head with sound rock** downstream — throws the jet clear |
| **Roller bucket** | Tailwater deeper than the sequent depth |
| **Plunge pool** | High dams; the jet falls into a scoured or excavated pool |

**The choice is governed by the TAILWATER level:**

> A **stilling basin needs adequate tailwater** to form the jump. If the tailwater is too low the jump sweeps out of the basin and scours the bed; too high and it is submerged, dissipating less.
> A **flip bucket** works where the tailwater is **inadequate** for a jump — it throws the jet far downstream, where it plunges into a pool and dissipates by air entrainment and turbulence. It requires **sound rock** at the impact point, since it will scour whatever is there.

**USBR stilling basin types II, III and IV** are selected by the **incoming Froude number**, with **chute blocks, baffle blocks and an end sill** proportioned accordingly. Baffle blocks are omitted at high velocities because **cavitation would destroy them**.

**The design flood.** For a large dam the spillway is sized on the **Probable Maximum Flood (PMF)** or a very long return period (1000 years and above), because the **consequence of failure is catastrophic** and no meaningful probability of exceedance is acceptable. For smaller structures a 100-year flood may suffice. **IS 11223** classifies dams by size and hazard and prescribes the design flood accordingly.

sections.heading: Earth and rockfill dams
sections.body:
**Types:**

| Type | Character |
|---|---|
| **Homogeneous** | One material throughout; only for **low** dams |
| **Zoned** | An **impervious core** flanked by pervious **shells** — the standard for any significant height |
| **Diaphragm** | A thin impervious membrane (concrete, steel, geomembrane) within a pervious fill |
| **Rockfill with impervious face** | Concrete-faced rockfill dam (CFRD) — increasingly common |

**The zoned section is the standard**, and the division of function is the point:

| Zone | Function |
|---|---|
| **Core** (clay or silty clay) | **Impermeability** — it stops the water |
| **Shells** (sand, gravel, rock) | **STRENGTH and stability** — they hold the core in place |
| **Filters** (graded, between core and shells) | **Prevent the core material migrating** into the shell voids (piping) |
| **Drainage** — chimney drain, horizontal blanket, toe drain | **Control the seepage line** and relieve pore pressure |
| Riprap / slope protection on the upstream face | Resists **wave action** |

**The filter is the component whose omission causes failure**, and its criterion is the same as any drainage filter: **coarse enough to pass water freely, fine enough to retain the adjacent soil**. Without it, seepage carries fine core particles into the coarse shell, forming a pipe that enlarges progressively — **internal erosion**, the mechanism behind a large share of embankment dam failures.

**Causes of failure — and the ranking matters:**

| Class | Causes | Share |
|---|---|---|
| **HYDRAULIC** | **OVERTOPPING**, wave erosion, erosion of the downstream toe, gully erosion | **The LARGEST cause — about a third** |
| **SEEPAGE** | **Piping (internal erosion)** through the dam or foundation, sloughing, excessive leakage | About a third |
| **STRUCTURAL** | **Slope failure** (upstream or downstream), foundation slide, settlement, earthquake damage | The remainder |

> **OVERTOPPING is the leading single cause of earth dam failure**, which is why **generous free board** and **adequate spillway capacity** are the first requirements — an earth dam has no reserve against overtopping at all, since flowing water erodes it immediately.

**The phreatic line (seepage line)** is the top flow line of the seepage through the dam body, and controlling it is central to the design:

> It is approximated by **Casagrande's parabola**, and it **must be kept within the body of the dam and away from the downstream slope**.

**Why.** If the phreatic line emerges on the **downstream slope**, seepage water exits there, the soil becomes saturated and its effective stress falls, and the slope **sloughs** progressively. The remedy is a **chimney (inclined) filter drain** and a **horizontal drainage blanket**, which intercept the seepage and bring it safely down to a **toe drain** — deliberately drawing the phreatic line down and away from the face.

**Slope stability — the critical conditions**, and each slope has its own:

| Slope | Critical condition | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **UPSTREAM** | **SUDDEN DRAWDOWN** | The water supporting the slope is removed while the **pore pressures inside are still high** — the worst combination of reduced support and reduced effective stress |
| **DOWNSTREAM** | **STEADY SEEPAGE** at full reservoir | Maximum pore pressure within the downstream portion |
| **Both** | **End of construction** | High **construction pore pressures** in a clay core that has not yet consolidated |
| Both | **Earthquake**, combined with the above | Inertia forces plus possible pore pressure build-up |

**Sudden drawdown is the condition candidates forget**, and it is worth understanding why it is so severe: during drawdown the reservoir level falls faster than the pore water can drain from the low-permeability core and shell, so the slope carries the **full weight of saturated soil with high internal pore pressure but no external water pressure to support it**. Minimum factors of safety are typically **1.5** for steady seepage and **1.2–1.3** for drawdown and seismic cases.

**Foundation treatment:**

| Measure | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Cut-off trench** filled with core material | Extends the impervious core into the foundation |
| **Grout curtain** | Reduces foundation permeability in rock |
| **Sheet pile or diaphragm wall** | Positive cut-off in alluvium |
| **Upstream impervious blanket** | Lengthens the seepage path where a full cut-off is impracticable |
| **Relief wells and toe drains** | Relieve foundation pore pressure downstream |
| Removal of unsuitable material | Organic, loose or compressible layers |

**Instrumentation and monitoring** are part of the design, not an afterthought: **piezometers** (pore pressure), **settlement gauges and inclinometers** (movement), **seepage measurement weirs** at the toe, and **seismographs**. Their purpose is to detect the **onset** of a problem — a rising piezometric level, an increase in seepage, or seepage that becomes **cloudy** (carrying soil, hence internal erosion in progress) — while there is still time to act. **Cloudy seepage is an emergency**, and recognising it as such is a genuine professional obligation.

**Compaction control** is where an embankment dam is actually made or lost. The core is compacted **slightly wet of optimum moisture content**, which produces a **dispersed** soil structure of **lower permeability** and better resistance to cracking; the shells are compacted for **strength**. Every layer is tested for **field density against the laboratory maximum**, and the specification is enforced layer by layer — because a single badly compacted layer becomes a preferential seepage path through the whole dam.

formulas.label: Water pressure on a dam
formulas.expression: P = ½ γ H², acting at H/3 above the base
formulas.note: The primary overturning force, resisted by the dam's own weight.

formulas.label: No tension (middle third) rule
formulas.note: Tension at the heel would open a crack, admitting full reservoir pressure and propagating the failure.

formulas.label: Sliding and overturning factors
formulas.expression: sliding: μΣV/ΣH ≥ 1.5 (shear friction factor 3–5) ;   overturning: ΣM_stabilising/ΣM_overturning ≥ 1.5
formulas.note: Uplift reduces ΣV and therefore both factors — which is why grout curtains and drainage galleries matter.

formulas.label: Elementary profile of a gravity dam
formulas.expression: B = H/√(S_c − c) ;   with no uplift B = H/√S_c
formulas.note: Follows directly from the no-tension condition. Full uplift widens the base substantially.

formulas.label: Ogee spillway discharge
formulas.note: The 3/2 exponent applies to every rectangular-type weir. √H is never a weir exponent.

formulas.label: Ogee profile principle
formulas.expression: The crest follows the LOWER NAPPE of a freely falling jet at the design head
formulas.note: So pressure on the crest stays atmospheric — no negative pressure, no cavitation, no loss of capacity.

formulas.label: Earth dam critical slope conditions
formulas.expression: UPSTREAM: sudden drawdown.   DOWNSTREAM: steady seepage.   BOTH: end of construction, and earthquake.
formulas.note: F ≥ 1.5 for steady seepage, 1.2–1.3 for drawdown and seismic.

formulas.label: Phreatic line
formulas.expression: Approximated by Casagrande's parabola; must be kept WITHIN the dam and away from the downstream slope
formulas.note: Achieved by a chimney filter drain, horizontal blanket and toe drain.

formulas.label: Leading cause of earth dam failure
formulas.expression: HYDRAULIC — overtopping above all; then seepage (piping); then structural (slope failure)
formulas.note: An earth dam has no reserve against overtopping, hence generous free board and spillway capacity.
